full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff Dhamai Tea Company Ltd. filed T.S. No. 76/58 in the Court of the Munsif, Second Court, Moulvi Bazar on the allegations inter alia that in consideration of the services rendered by the defendant no. 1 as an employee of the plaintiff, the latter allowed the defendant to hold the agricultural suit land measuring 10 bigha 7 kathas and 9 chattels situated within the tea estate itself as a licensee thereof at the licence fee of Re. 1 per bigha per year. He was to occupy the said land as long as he was in the service of the plaintiff with yearly renewals. He executed licence documents. The defendant was dismissed from the service of the plaintiff in July, 1956. As he did not vacate the land on demand the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession-The Government was the defendant no. 2 in the suit. 

 4. The defence of the defendant no. 1 in both the suits was that, he was a watchman of the plaintiff. The suit land in T.S No. 76/58 was leased out to him by Mr. Hithford, the then Manager of the plaintiff Company at the rate of Re. 1 per bigas per year 31/32 years back. He has possessed the suit land as a tenant paying rent thereof. He has acquired tenancy right in the suit land and is not liable to be evicted. He denied execution of any license document. He hold the homestead which is the subject matter of T.S. No. 98/58 as nonkar tenant as he rendered services to the plaintiff. He built all the huts in question at his own cost. After the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 he held the land as tenant under the Government. He is, therefore, not liable to be evicted. The defendant No. 2, the then Government of East Pakistan entered appearance but did not contest the suits. 

 5. The Munsif, Second Court, Moulvi Bazar, tried the two suits analogously and by the same judgment dated 19.6.61 dismissed T.S. No. 76/58 on the finding that the document in question Ext. 1(c) relied upon by the plaintiff was a lease and not a licence and that the defendant No. 1 had tenancy right in the agricultural land. He decreed T.S. no. 98/58 on the finding that the defendant No. 1 occupied the quarters and the land as a licensee and not as a tenant of the plaintiff. 

 9. Mr. Hafizullah, learned Advocate for  this finding the appellant, contend that of the appellate Court below is not correct, as it has applied the law relating to documents executed by a pardanashin and illiterate lady to the instant case. The defendant no.1 was a male worker and not a pardanshin and illiterate lady. He has not complained in his written statement and in his deposition that his thumb impression was obtained without his knowing of the contents of the document. This objection must be sustained. It is, however, a different matter as to how far the document in question Ext. 1(c) will govern the transaction, to which I shall advert later. 

 10. The appellate Court then found that the defendant no.1 has been in possession of the suit land for the last 25/26 years. It found that the defendant no. 1 has been described as a tenant and the amount paid by him has been described as rent in Ext. 3, a rent record book, in Exts. C, C(1) and C(2), counterfoils of rent receipts and in Ext. A-A(5), the rent-receipts. The counterfoils and rent-receipts are forms of receipt maintained under rule 75 of section 72 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 which strongly suggest a tenancy. Further, in the plaint itself the transaction in question has been described as a lease in more than one place. The appellate Court below then noticed some of the provisions of the agreement in question Ext. 1(c). In clause I thereof the defendants was authorised "to hold" the set it land. The appellate Court interpreted the word "hold" to mean occupation and keeping possession of the suit land. The words used in the document, according to the appellate Court, indicate that a lease was granted to the defendant. The uninterrupted possession of the suit land for the last 25 years suggests that the defendant was given exclusive possession of the suit land. There is no evidence on record that the plaintiff ever executed any act of ownership over the suit land during the period in which the defendant was in possession of it the defendant's exclusive possession suggest a lease. The plaintiff took the plea that the suit land, admittedly situated within the tea estate itself, cannot be leased out. Under the Explanation to section 1 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 land included in a tea estate is excluded from the operation of the said Act if it is let out for the maintenance of the coolies working on the cultivation. The plaintiff pleaded that the defendant No. 1 was a coolie and the suit land was licensed out to him for his maintenance. The appellate Court held that the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 applies to the suit land because the defendant No. 1 was not a coolie but a chowkidar. With the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent-receiving interest of the plaintiff in the suit land was acquired by the Government and the defendant No. 1 holds the suit land under the Government as a tenant. The defendant therefore cannot be evicted. 

 "The difference between a tenancy and a licence is, therefore, that in tenancy an interest passes in the land, whereas in a licence it does not. In distinguishing between them, a crucial test has sometimes been supposed to be whether the occupier has exclusive possession or not. If he was let into exclusive possession, he was said to be a tenant albeit only a tenant at will......whereas, if he had not exclusive possession he was only a licensee. This test has however often given rise to misgivings because it may not correspond to realities. The test of exclusive possession is by no means decisive." 

 "After discussing some instances lately of occupiers in exclusive possession who have been held to be not tenants but only licensees Denning, L.J. further observes as follows:- "The result of all these cases is that, although a person who is let into exclusive possession is, prima facie, to be considered to be a tenant nevertheless he will not be held to be so if the circumstances negative any intention to create a tenancy. Words alone may not suffice. Parties cannot turn a tenancy into licence merely by calling it one. But if the circumstances and the conduct of the parties show that all that was intended was that the occupier should be granted a personal privilege with no interest in the land he will be held only to a licensee." 

 22. This view of exclusive possession has not been accepted as of general application by Jenkins, L.J. in Addiscombe Garden Estates Ltd. and another Vs. Crabbe & others, (1957) 3 All E.R. 563. Referring to Denning, L.J.s dictum in Errington Vs. Errington (previously cited) that "the test of exclusive possession is by no means decisive." His Lordship says "I think that wide statement must be treated as qualified by his (Denning, L.J.'s) observations in Facchini Vs. Bryson (1952) 1 T.L.R. at P. 1389) and it seems to me that save in exceptional cases of the kind mentioned by Denning L.J., is that case, the law remains that the fact of exclusive possession, if not decisive against the view that there is a mere licence as distinct from a tenancy, is at all events a consideration of the first importance." 

 "There has been something in the circumstances such as a family arrangement, an act of friendship or generosity or the like, to negative any intention to create a tenancy. In such circumstances it would be obviously unjust to saddle the owner with a tenancy, with all the momentous consequences that entails now-a-days, when there was no intention to create a tenancy at all. 

 25. In favour of the plaintiff, all that can be said is that had the defendant No. 1 not been an employee of the plaintiff there would have been no occasion to grant him the suit land at all. True, but the plaintiff has led no evidence as to how initially the defendant No. I came upon the suit land. P.W.1 has stated that the previous licenses are destroyed. P.W 4, the manager of the tea estate admits, "There were of course some tenanted lands outside the land of the tea plantation area but within the orbit of the Dhamai Tea Estate as a whole." If that is so, the claim of the defendant No. 1 to be a tenant of the suit land is not a claim inconsistent with the practice of the plaintiff-company. In such a situation, I fail to see how the plaintiff's case comes within the category of cases referred to by Denning, L.J. 

 26. It appears to me that the proposition that the test of exclusive possession is by no means decisive cannot be said to be of general application. The principle must be limited to the kinds of cases mentioned by Denning, L.J. in Foschini's case and Errington's case (previously cited). Exclusive possession may not be a decisive test in favour of a tenancy, but it still remains a consideration of the first importance. 

 29. The defendant's exclusive possession is thus a strong pointer to tenancy. The other circumstances and conduct of the parties, as discussed by the appellate Court below, also indicate that the defendant was treated by the plaintiff as a tenant and the payment made by the defendant was treated as rent. Mr. Hafizullah has made no submissions on the appellate Court's treatment of Exts. 3a, C, C (1) and C(2) and A-A(5). His submission was that these exhibits ought not to have been given prime consideration and the case ought to have been decided on an interpretation of Ext. 1 (c) alone, to which I have already adverted. In that of the matter I find no ground for interference in S.A. No. 27/66.
